title: Local autonomous inference machines for quantum LDPC codes
abstract: We introduce a local and distributed framework for decoding quantum LDPC codes. Built atop belief propagation (BP), the architecture combines strictly local processing of syndrome information, local feedback, autonomous operation, and highly parallelized decoding. We establish the framework at two complementary levels. First, we show that any code exhibiting a threshold under iterative BP decoding can be promoted to an autonomous local measurement-and-feedback dynamics while preserving that threshold. We then turn to codes for which naive BP does not itself exhibit threshold behavior. Our key observation is that BP can nevertheless provide sufficiently accurate \emph{local} marginal information: active syndrome defects use these local beliefs to \emph{move}, pair, and annihilate through asynchronous feedback. We demonstrate numerically that this construction exhibits threshold behavior in the point-like sectors of the two- and three-dimensional toric codes, where conventional BP decoding fails. Exploiting the graph-generality of BP, we then study the inference dynamics on the membrane-like sector of the three-dimensional toric code and in a family of bivariate-bicycle quantum LDPC codes.
summary: This work proposes a novel, local, and distributed inference machine for decoding quantum LDPC codes. By replacing global decoding steps with local, belief-guided measurements and feedback, the framework successfully demonstrates error correction threshold behavior in regimes where traditional Belief Propagation fails. This advances the feasibility of building fault-tolerant quantum computation using local physical processes.
main_problem: The paper addresses the challenge of developing a local and distributed framework for decoding quantum Low-Density Parity-Check (LDPC) codes, aiming to realize error correction as a local, non-equilibrium process.
main_result: The proposed local inference machine exhibits threshold behavior for quantum LDPC codes in sectors (like point-like sectors of the toric code) where conventional Belief Propagation (BP) decoding fails.
method: The authors construct an autonomous inference machine that uses local measurements and feedback based on local marginal information derived from BP, rather than requiring global consistency.
model_or_system: The system involves quantum LDPC codes defined on qubits, analyzed using a Tanner graph structure. The dynamics are modeled through local message passing, discrete time steps, and continuous-time Poisson clock updates.
key_observables: Decoding Threshold ($p_{th}$), Logical Error Rate ($p_L$), and Syndrome Clearing Time ($t_{clr}$).
important_parameters: Physical error rate ($p$), Code distance ($d$), and the local belief information ($	ext{Pr}_{	ext{BP}}(e_v|s)$).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the use of CSS quantum codes on qubits and relies on the local inference engine (BP) providing sufficient local marginal information even when globally inconsistent.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the local autonomous inference setup, showing error trajectories for repetition codes, and comparing $p_L$ vs $p$ and $t_{clr}$ for 2D and 3D toric codes under various noise conditions.
paper_structure: The paper first introduces the local autonomous inference framework, showing its equivalence to standard BP for some codes. It then demonstrates its effectiveness on codes where standard BP fails, analyzing dynamics in discrete and continuous time for various code geometries.
why_interesting: The concept of mapping complex quantum error correction tasks onto local, autonomous, feedback-driven dynamics is highly relevant to building physical quantum hardware, bridging theoretical quantum information with physical implementation constraints.
